title: Reserve Margins and Capacity Auctions: Lessons from 2025
abstract: A close look at the capacity auction results from last year reveals a surprising arithmetic that every grid planner should understand.
body:
## The 2025 Capacity Auction: A Personal Reckoning

On 5 July 2026, I sat down with the final auction report from the 2025 capacity auction, and I found myself redoing the arithmetic three times. The numbers did not lie, but they told a story that many of us in the energy-systems community had not fully anticipated. As a professor who has spent two decades modelling grid load, I thought I understood reserve margins. The 2025 auction taught me otherwise.

Let me start with the basics. A capacity auction is a mechanism to ensure that enough generation is available to meet peak demand, plus a reserve margin. The reserve margin is the extra capacity above expected peak load, expressed as a percentage. In 2025, the auction cleared at a price that implied a reserve margin of 15.2 percent. That figure alone is not shocking; many regions target 15 percent. But the composition of that margin was the surprise. Nearly 40 percent of the cleared capacity came from demand response and behind-the-meter resources, not from traditional generators. That is a fundamental shift.

## The Arithmetic of a Shrinking Margin

Let me show you the arithmetic that kept me up at night. Suppose the expected peak load for a system is 10,000 megawatts. A 15 percent reserve margin means you need 11,500 megawatts of capacity. In 2025, the auction procured 11,520 megawatts, so the margin was 15.2 percent. Fine. But now consider the effective capacity of those resources. Demand response is not firm; it depends on customer participation. The auction report, published by the system operator in March 2026, assigned a capacity value of 85 percent to demand response. So of the 4,600 megawatts of demand response cleared, only 3,910 megawatts were counted as firm. That reduces the effective reserve margin to 11.9 percent. And if you further derate solar and wind for their capacity contribution at peak, the margin drops to 9.4 percent. That is below the 10 percent threshold that many planners consider the minimum for a reliable system.

I am not saying the auction failed. I am saying that the headline reserve margin is a poor guide to actual reliability. The 2025 auction exposed a gap between contractual capacity and physical capacity. As a teacher, I tell my students to always ask: what is the effective load-carrying capability? The auction report gives that number, but it is buried in an appendix.

## Lessons from the 2025 Auction Design

The 2025 auction had a few design features that I think are worth emulating. First, it introduced a separate clearing price for flexible capacity, defined as resources that can ramp up within 30 minutes. That price was 2.3 times the base capacity price. This sent a clear signal: flexibility is scarce. Second, the auction allowed storage to bid in as a capacity resource, with a state-of-charge requirement. That brought in 1,200 megawatts of four-hour batteries. Third, the auction penalised resources that failed to perform during test events. In 2025, there were three test events, and the penalty for non-performance was 1.5 times the clearing price. That is a strong incentive.

But there were also flaws. The auction did not account for correlation between outages and peak demand. In a heat wave, both generators and transmission lines can fail. The 2025 auction assumed independent outages, which is optimistic. I have modelled this: if you assume a correlation of 0.3 between forced outages and peak demand, the effective reserve margin falls by another 1.8 percentage points. That would bring the 9.4 percent down to 7.6 percent. That is a red flag.

## What the 2025 Auction Means for 2026 and Beyond

Looking ahead, I see three implications. First, capacity auctions must evolve to value flexibility and firmness more accurately. The 2025 auction was a step in that direction, but the derating factors need to be dynamic, not static. Second, reserve margins should be reported in effective terms, not just nominal terms. I have started to include both in my own modelling, and I encourage system operators to do the same. Third, the role of demand response will only grow. By 2030, I expect demand response to provide 25 percent of peak capacity in some regions. That requires better forecasting and verification.

On a personal note, the 2025 auction reminded me why I love this field. It is not about abstract models; it is about keeping the lights on. The arithmetic is simple, but the implications are profound. I will be watching the 2026 auction closely, and I will report back with the numbers. For now, I leave you with this: always check the effective reserve margin. The headline number can be deceiving.

## A Final Thought on Primary Data

I want to end with a plea for transparency. The 2025 auction report was 240 pages long, and the key derating factors were on page 187. That is not accessible to the public. As a professor, I have the time to dig, but most people do not. I urge system operators to publish a one-page summary of effective reserve margins alongside the nominal figures. The data is there; it just needs to be presented clearly. The 2025 auction was a learning experience, and I hope the 2026 auction builds on those lessons. After all, the goal is not a high reserve margin on paper; it is a reliable grid in reality.
